name: Common Noun

dimensions.form: Noun stem; typically uncapitalized; takes number and case inflection
dimensions.meaning: Denotes class or category of entities; supports count/non-count distinction
dimensions.function: Head of Nom; provides descriptive content for reference
dimensions.distribution: Heads Nom in common NPs; modifier position in N-N compounds

1.definition: Provides a nominal description usable with ordinary NP determination when the count and number profile permits it

projection.target: A use like the tallest building can identify a unique referent while keeping a common lexical head. Identification alone therefore does not predict the distribution of a proper noun.
projection.evidence: CGEL separates proper-noun specialization from syntactic determination and reference.

curious.title: Words for kinds of things
curious.summary: Common nouns like dog and city name a kind or category, not one particular individual.
curious.body:
Dog and city are common nouns. Each names a class or category of things. Common nouns take endings for number (dog, dogs) and are typically written without a capital letter.

A common noun can still lead to one particular thing. In the tallest building, the phrase can pick out a single building, yet building is still a common noun. Picking out one thing doesn't, by itself, make a word a name.
curious.try: Pick a word for a kind of thing in the room. Does it also name one particular thing, or the whole kind?

teacher.summary: Teaches the basic noun category, and how it differs from the proper noun.
teacher.explain: A common noun denotes a class or category of entities. It is the head of a nominal, supplies descriptive content for reference, takes number and case inflection, and supports the count and non-count distinction. Dog and city are this dictionary's examples. The pattern provides a nominal description usable with ordinary determination when the count and number profile permits it. Identification alone doesn't make a noun proper: the tallest building can identify a unique referent while keeping a common noun as its head. Compare with the proper noun, a parallel noun category.
teacher.terms: Common noun is the traditional term and the one used here. Countable and uncountable nouns are sometimes called count and non-count nouns; this dictionary prefers non-count.

contrasts.note: Identifies one building, but the head word building is still a common noun.

watch_for: A learner might treat a noun as proper whenever a phrase points to one individual, such as the tallest building.
A learner might assume every common noun can follow a cardinal number, though this dictionary says the count and number profile has to permit it.
teacher.activity: Students list five common nouns from the classroom. For each, they say whether it can follow a, much or a cardinal number, then compare lists with a partner.

child.hook: Which words name a kind of thing, like dog?
child.explain: Words like dog and city name a kind of thing. They don't name just one special one. Even in the tallest building, the main word is still building.
child.play: Look around. Say five words for kinds of things, like chair or tree. Then say one special name for each, like a friend's name for their pet.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Common Noun." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/n-common-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, 5c11b28).
